content: Operators in situations where the control authorities are not available in the receiving country must adhere to specific protocols to ensure the proper handling and distribution of controlled substances. Suppliers should be limited to those recognized by the control authorities of exporting countries. These suppliers must meet the following criteria: 1. They must have sufficient experience in supplying high-quality emergency medical supplies. 2. They should possess managerial capability to evaluate the appropriateness of requests for simplified procedures from operators. 3. They must maintain an adequate stock level and employ a responsible pharmacist. 4. They should have comprehensive knowledge of relevant international conventions. 5. They must have a standard agreement with the control authorities of exporting countries. The standard agreement between suppliers and the control authorities of exporting countries should include: 1. Criteria for accepting shipment requests from operators, specifying the essential information to be provided to the supplier. If the operator is also a supplier, the agreement will be between the operator and the control authorities. 2. A pre-determined list of credible operators, who must be established organizations with adequate experience in international humanitarian medical assistance, responsible medical management (e.g., medical doctors or pharmacists), and appropriate logistical support. 3. A statement from the operator or, if applicable, a UN agency, detailing the nature of the emergency. 4. Mechanisms to prevent diversion of supplies after delivery. 5. Identification of recipients in the receiving country, as far as possible. If control authorities are available in the receiving country, they should be notified promptly by the control authorities of the exporting country and the operator about the emergency delivery. Import authorization may not be required under emergency circumstances. Suppliers are responsible for informing the control authorities of the exporting country about each emergency shipment in response to an operator's request, allowing for intervention if necessary. They must also submit an annual report to the control authorities of the exporting country, detailing emergency deliveries, quantities of drugs involved, and their destinations. This report should be duplicated so that one copy can be forwarded to the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB). Additionally, suppliers or operators, through the suppliers, must report any problems encountered in the emergency delivery process to the control authorities of the exporting countries, with a copy sent to the INCB. The operator's role includes submitting a written request for emergency supplies of controlled substances to the supplier using the provided model form. The operator is responsible for: Providing accurate information on the form. Handling controlled drugs at the receiving end or ensuring their delivery to reliable recipients. Reporting to the control authorities of the receiving country (if available) as soon as possible. Reporting unused quantities to the control authorities of the receiving country or arranging for the end-user to do so. Reporting any issues encountered in the emergency delivery process to the control authorities of the exporting country through the supplier, with a copy sent to the INCB. The supplier's role involves verifying that the nature of the emergency justifies the application of the simplified procedure without requiring export/import authorizations. Suppliers must: Immediately submit a copy of the shipment request to the control authorities of the exporting country. Submit an annual report on emergency deliveries, including quantities of drugs involved and their destinations, with a copy sent to the INCB. Report any problems encountered in the emergency delivery process to the control authorities of the exporting country, with a copy sent to the INCB. The control authorities of the exporting country must inform their counterparts in the receiving country (if available) about the emergency deliveries. The control authorities of the receiving country have the right to refuse the importation of such deliveries. Emergency deliveries are not included in the receiving country's estimate, as they are considered to have been consumed in the exporting country. Recognizing that some controlled drugs, such as opioid analgesics, are essential medicines for alleviating human suffering, it is critical to ensure timely international supplies of these medicines during humanitarian emergencies. However, the established international drug control system often complicates the rapid transportation of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances to emergency sites. Simplified control procedures are justified in such situations to facilitate the transportation and provision of these essential medicines. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) have emphasized the importance of addressing these challenges through intensified dialogue between health and drug control authorities at all levels. Member States are urged to establish simplified regulatory procedures to enable the timely international supply of controlled substances during emergencies. The WHO, in consultation with relevant United Nations bodies, is tasked with preparing model guidelines to assist national authorities in developing such procedures.
